utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Madam Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is the case IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. Let me greet you on behalf of the Trial Chamber since you're now taking over from the previous court deputy. On behalf of all my colleagues, let me welcome you into this courtroom and trial proceedings. Today we are going to start with the Prlic Defence closing arguments, but before we do so, let me flag out a little technical problem. Madam Registrar told me that we still have problems with LiveNote. There might be a problem if Mr. Karnavas planned to display documents, but apparently we're going to get hard copies if there are any documents. So even if we're not supposed to -- or not able to see the document on our screens, we'll have a hard copy of it. Otherwise, as Madam Registrar told me, we would have to wait for another 25 minutes because we would have to reboot the entire IT system. So, Mr. Karnavas, is that going to cause you a problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, and everyone in and around the courtroom. No, it will not cause me a problem at this moment. I regret to say that we don't have hard copies. I will not be referring to any hard copies at this moment, for the next 20 minutes to 30 minutes. I must say this has been sort of a Herculean task trying to get ready for this, and we've had some technical problems of our own, and in light of what happened last week, we tried to downsize, but we were not able to do our copying on time, but we will proceed in an orderly fashion and hopefully everyone will be able to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Karnavas. Last week the Stojic Defence had seized the legal officer of an issue connected with the fact that there might be an accused wishing to speak at the end of their closing arguments. Judge Trechsel is going to tell everybody what the Trial Chamber's view is on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Prosecution, counsel for the Defence, a certain lack of clarity reigns with regard to the organisation of the time between counsel and accused, and it would be arrogant if I took all the blame because I'm not alone here, but I take as much as you want to attribute to me. The solution we have again discussed about is the following: As we have always said, five hours per Defence. Normally this is the hour for counsel pleading. If one Defence has a strong wish of the accused himself to take part in the pleadings, counsel can leave up to 30 minutes to the accused in person. The Chamber would be grateful if counsel would advise the Chamber of whether this will be the case and at what point in the proceedings. After we have heard all six Defences, the question arises whether the Prosecution asks for time for rebuttal. If so, the Chamber will decide how much time to allocate and will give a corresponding amount of time to Defences. It is possible, as Mr. Scott last week has indicated that he has said his last word in this case in this Chamber. In that case, normally there would be no opportunity for rebuttal for the Defences. However, the Chamber is aware of the fact that we do not have a monolithic block of one Defence but we have six accused, and our experience leads us to allow for the possibility that one Defence may shift responsibility attributed to the accused to another accused, so that after having heard all Defences, it is not excluded that one Defence feels a strong urge to reply to another Defence. The Chamber is prepared to hear reasoned applications and if it is convinced, it will give the possibility for a rebuttal within the Defences. The Prosecutor would not come in any more, and no counsel will be allowed to take the floor more than once. Then the proceedings under Rule 86(A) are closed, and as we are all of continental procedural background and have certain principles that are almost regarded as holy in our countries, we are prepared to afford to the accused personally the possibility to have the last word. This is almost a sacred principle for us, and although it's not provided for in the Rules, I think nobody can really feel aggrieved that we plan to do this. That's all. I hope that this is clear, and if not, again I take the blame and would be prepared to clarify. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: President Antonetti, Judge Prandler, Judge Trechsel, Judge Mindua, good afternoon, and good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom and anyone who may be watching these proceedings outside the courtroom. Closing argument, also known as summation, is perhaps the most exciting stage of the proceedings for a trial advocate. It's the opportunity for the advocate to show and display his oratorial skills, the craft of narrating a persuasive narrative that carries the day. He wants the Judges or the trier of fact if it's a injury, to be mesmerised by every word that the advocate is saying. In fact, closing arguments is considered so significant that when we're learning the craft, we're told never ever tell the trier of fact that what you're saying is not evidence. You want the Judges to believe or the jury to believe that what you're saying is the evidence. Well, for the first time, in my career at least, I'm going to break away from that tradition, and I will urge the Trial Chamber to be ever-mindful that what we are saying here today and what we have said in our final briefs is not evidence. It is not evidence. It's argument. It's perhaps what we may want the Trial Chamber to accept, to believe, and to act upon, but it is not evidence, not what I say, not what the Prosecutor said, or what my colleagues will say. Neither is what is contained in the final briefs. We've spent close to five years in this courtroom. We have a transcript of 52.000 pages. We have 9.000 documents. That's the record, and in there lies the truth. In there lies the answers that you must seek in making a final determination. However imperfect the record may be, and we may disagree on whether everything came in that we wanted to be part of the record, and I -- I don't think that there is a single person here or party that is absolutely satisfied, but that's the way it goes. The record is what it is, and personal knowledge or preconceived impressions or popular assumptions of what is believed to be fact is not the record. And had the Trial Chamber instructed us to limit ourselves to one and only one sentence, albeit we could use a semicolon to stretch it out a little bit, I would say pay close scrutiny and attention to the record, the entire record. Therein lies the answers to whatever -- to whether the Prosecution has proved every element of each and every count beyond a reasonable doubt. And that would be it. Effectively, or I should say essentially, our job is finished here. We may wax eloquently, but the real job, the real task at hand is before you, because you have to go through the record. Now, the Prosecution stressed that the Defence, and it seemed as if it was a universal declaration, that we parsed words. We selected snippets of documents and conveniently and creatively took facts out of context. I don't speak for the Defence. I speak for Dr. Jadranko Prlic, and I can assure Your Honours that we take exception. Ms. Tomanovic and I categorically reject this assertion, and we submit that these are calculated tactics to deflect and misguide. Now, in reading the Prosecution's final brief, in listening to the closing arguments by these very, very talented and skilful Prosecutors, I was reminded of the opening lines delivered by Socrates in his closing argument which has faithfully been recorded by Plato in the "Apology": "How you must felt, O men of Athens, if hearing the speeches of my accusers I cannot tell, but I know that their persuasive words almost made me forget who I was, such was the effect of them, and yet they have hardly spoken a word of truth." The manner in which evidence was assembled by the Prosecution in the final brief, at least insofar as Dr. Jadranko Prlic is concerned, is, at a minimum, disquieting. The Prosecution seeks to convict Dr. Prlic by contorting the facts into a procrustean bed, and sadly, it would appear, that the Prosecution has forsaken its role to seek justice, not merely to convict. The United States Supreme Court in Burger v. United States reminds us all that while the Prosecution may strike hard, it is not at liberty to strike foul. Now, in preparing for my closing arguments, I came across a text, "A Modern Legal Ethics: Adversary Advocacy in a Democratic Age," and Yale Professor Daniel Markovits writes as follows: "Distinctive professional commitments of prosecutors may also be understood, from within legal ethics, as reflecting the fact that rather than representing an ordinary client before a neutral tribunal, the prosecutor represents one arm of the state before another. At least in principle, the state has no proper interest in victory for its own sake because it should never pursue injustice. The state does not need a bulwark against authority because it is the authority. The prosecutor's distinctive commitment to the truth and fairness, therefore, elaborates a role whose genetic structure departs from the structure of adversary advocacy." And I think this is exactly what Judge Hunt was referring to in his refrain to all of us, and I believe in particular to his fellow brethren and to this institution in its legacy when he said: "The Tribunal will not be judged by the number of convictions it enters but by the fairness of its trials. The duties and responsibilities of the Prosecutor differ from and are wider than the Defence. This is unequivocally spelled out in the ICTY standards of professional conduct for Prosecutor counsel." And we see that in Article 2, and I quote where it says that the Prosecutor is duty-bound to "assist the Tribunal to arrive at the truth and to do justice for the international community, victims, and the accused." And if I may quote from Robert Jackson as well, he reminded an audience of federal prosecutors when he was the Attorney General of the United States back in 1940: "Your positions are of such independence and importance that while you are being diligent, strict, and vigorous in law enforcement, you can also afford to be just." The Prosecution in this case as in any other case before the ICTY represents one organ of the Tribunal before another, and this Tribunal represents by virtue of its creator and its sustainer the United Nations, humanity itself. Thus in principle, the ICTY should not and does not have an interest in the Prosecution's victory for its own sake despite that appalling sign that hangs in the lobby of this august institution informing all visitors as they walk in the mission of this institution, the raison d'etre of this Tribunal, and I quote, "Bring war criminals to justice," as opposed to just saying that this institution is for justice. Sadly, that's the same motto you will find when you open up the ICTY web site. The United Nations should not and does not have an interest in a victory for its own sake despite the enormous amount of money it has spent trying this case, and as the Prosecution should not be pushing -- pursuing sharp practices that are designed to obfuscate or conceal the truth for the sake of winning the case, and I've noted that in the past, we should be given the needle, not the haystack. The members of the Trial Chamber should not shy away and should not equivocate in their obligation to hold the Prosecution to the task of carrying out their burden and evaluating the evidence with equal measure and standard. There is no balancing test to be applied in order to even the odds, even though the odds are stacked against the Defence. The Prosecution enjoys no special privileges because it is a member of the ICTY and, by extension, a member of the UN. Now, in keeping with the instructions of the Trial Chamber, we will focus our closing arguments on responding to the sections of the Prosecution's final brief primarily related to Dr. Prlic found in paragraphs 361 to 526. We will also be touching on other parts of the final brief and the closing arguments, though - and it's not complaint, but just an observation - five hours is about one hour per year. A lot of work to do, and however we were able to slice it and dice it, we basically found ourselves in a very difficult situation to try to get everything done and to go over the entire brief, and that's not going to be our intention at this point. Nor is our intention to shift the blame or to deflect responsibility. Dr. Prlic does not shy away from any of the decisions he signed on behalf of the temporary executive authority, the HVO HZ-HB in his capacity as the president. He was unambiguous and categorical on this matter when he gave his statement back on the 5th of May, 2008. These decisions and these conclusions, and the Prosecution can use these catchy phrases like "the Prlic decision," "the Prlic ultimatum," "the Prlic-Stojic proclamation." More like titles out of a Robert Ludlum book. They can do that all they want. The end of the day, those decisions were of the collective, and the collective was responsible for taking these decisions. Dr. Prlic signed those decisions, and he's not shying away from the fact that he took part of and signed all of those decisions. Now, in saying that, I must say with some regret that those decisions were also part of the decisions taken by Accused Bruno Stojic. If I may paraphrase Ms. West's eloquent submissions, it is wholly unrewarding exercise in linguistics gymnastics for Mr. Stojic, in this case, to claim that the appointments signed by Dr. Prlic were Prlic appointments as opposed to HVO HZ-HB appointments that were made after Mr. Stojic, among all the other members of the HVO HZ-HB, had voted on them. And I'm referring to paragraphs 286, 302, and 307 of the briefs. Although we've heard so much testimony on that, whose appointments were they, what was the power or the authority behind the signature. And The same thing goes with the decision, including the decision -- all of the decisions, including the decision on 15 January 1993. While we submit that the decision was made after a good-faith belief that what had been represented by General Praljak was true, accurate, and complete, and that the decision on its face is neither illegal nor sinister in keeping with what was happening, keeping in mind that in Geneva you have negotiators that are negotiating and some are -- the negotiators are encouraging at least two of the parties to try to reach an agreement and the negotiations continue on to Zagreb; considering the events that were happening elsewhere, where allies were actually at each other and not focusing on the real danger, on the real front; so while that decision on its face was neither illegal nor sinister, for Mr. Stojic now to claim that it was the Prlic decision, in paragraph 165, incidentally, among elsewhere, is not a -- is not only wholly unrewarding, but it's counter-productive because there's so much evidence on this issue. And its even contradicted by his own witnesses who came in and testified as to how decisions were reached and whose decisions they were. And I submit it is irrationally exuberant to assume that these sorts of tactics yield anything other than fool's gold for anybody. Shifting responsibility for trying to hide by any party or parsing out words will not yield benefits, especially since there are -- there is evidence. And an advocate has the responsibility, has the responsibility, according to -- if I may quote Henry Lord Brougham in 1820 in Queen's Caroline's case, he says: "An advocate in the discharge of his duty knows but one person in all the world and that person is the client, to save that client by all means and expedience and at all hazards and costs to other persons, in amongst them to himself. That's his first and only duty, and in performing this duty he must not regard the alarm, the torments, the destructions which he may bring upon others." In other words, counsel is expected to display a degree of zeal in his representation, and of course in doing so we're all required not to overstep certain boundaries, and I hope and I pray that during my representation of Dr. Prlic in the last five years, although I have tested everyone's patience no doubt, that I haven't overstepped that boundary in representing and zealously representing Dr. Prlic. Now, before I turn to the section relating to Dr. Prlic, it merits focusing a little bit on the Prosecution's assertions in paragraph 3 of the final brief. In its remarks during the closing arguments, and on specifically speaking about the remarks about Defence witnesses because they were Croats. Now, there was this caveat that they're insiders, and of course it was said, "Well, in principle, nothing's wrong with that. Croats have every much right to appear in this institution and give testimony as anyone else," but given that the Prosecution considers them as insiders, every single one of them, without exception, basically, and of course it would go without saying that they're part and parcel of the alleged JCE, they're asking the Trial Chamber to discount their testimony, to ignore their testimony. Now, the Prosecution has worked very hard in this case, and they're honourable people, and you cannot be in this case without getting a little bit subjective. I think I've been accused of that. But I have to say, and I say this with all regret, it actually pains me to say this, that throughout the final argument, we heard or there was this undertone of this dark and unseemly theme that permeated throughout the closing argument, at least that's how it was perceived, and keep in mind the shoes in which the accused sit here, and keep in mind that the extension of the accused are all the witnesses that came to testify on their behalf, but this dark and unseemly theme was Croat equals Nationalist, equals Ustasha, equals Nazi. That's how it was perceived. Perhaps it wasn't meant that way. Perhaps it was just using examples. But I dare say that the -- this -- this theme that ran so deep and so long and so consistent throughout their presentation was disquieting. And imagine if I were to come into this courtroom and say don't trust Muslim witnesses. Don't give them any credibility, because obviously they're going to be sympathisers of the Muslim cause that Izetbegovic, Silajdzic, Ganic and the rest were pursuing, that would be shameful. I think and I submit that witnesses should be judged not on the basis of their religious origin, their occupation, or professional affiliation. Simply because a witness is a non-Croat or is affiliated with a UN or EU or some international organisation, or comes or originates from a country that happens to be a permanent member of the Security Council, does that mean that they start with a score of 100 per cent credibility and then Croats that appear on behalf of the Defence start with zero? No witness gets a free pass. No witness is more credible than another on the basis of the criteria the Prosecution seem to be suggesting, and no witness should benefit or suffer from preconditions or prejudice simply based on whose behalf they appear. The witnesses who testified on behalf of Dr. Prlic were not without substance and accomplishments. All held high responsible positions. We had a former prime minister. We had several former ambassadors. We had a minister of finance of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We had a former minister of foreign affairs for the Republic of Croatia who had served as ambassador to the United States. And let me park here. Why is he less credible than, say, Galbraith, who took the stand and admitted that during the embargo the US was breaking it and he was assisting in his capacity as ambassador of the United States? So why are the Croat witnesses less credible than the Prosecution witnesses? The list goes on as far as all of the witnesses that testified on behalf of Dr. Prlic, and they were tested. They were tested under cross-examination. We did not submit any statements that were crafted over a period of days - and I'm going to talk about that a little bit - and then submit them as part of the direct examination of the witness. I have a lot to say about that. I've said it before, and I apologise, but you may have to hear it again, and I think it's important, because it goes to the weight to be given to the witness. The Prosecution dismisses the Defence witnesses and denigrates them publicly as hardcore nationalists committed to the cause of reconstituting the 1939 Banovina. And then they ask you, Your Honours, to do likewise, and we urge you to treat all witnesses with equal care and equal consideration and just examine the record. And the record means everything. It don't mean just the Prosecution's direct examination or just the Prosecution's cross-examination. We used to have this wonderful rule here. It was called 98 bis. Based on the Anglo-Saxon principle of submitting a motion for a judgement of acquittal after the Prosecution put on its entire case. If they didn't meet their burden at that stage, then counts or the entire case could be thrown out; the principle being that, the Prosecution carrying the burden would have to go forward and put on its case. Well, for a variety of reasons, none of which make sense to me, but I don't count, we didn't get rid of the Rule. We kept the Rule, but we took the teeth out of it. So now we submit a 98 bis brief, or some parties do, which I consider nothing other than a reconfirmation of the indictment. Why? Because you're asked to disregard everything that came in from the Defence, all the cross-examination, all the documents. Just look at what the Prosecutor presented and then see whether based on that a reasonable trier of fact could find a guilty verdict. Well, what's the purpose? That's the same standard, Your Honours, I submit, that Judges use in confirming indictments. It's the same standard. And then if you want to add a little salt to the injury, after they win the 98 bis, then all of a sudden the case has gotten stronger. It was the same case. You never bothered to look at the Defence evidence. But now we're saying the record, the record, is everything. So on direct examination, you want to pay close attention to the answer, not to the question, because the question, if it's suggestive, then the answer doesn't have much value. On cross-examination, however, we submit, and I know it's somewhat different here in Europe or for some Judges who come from the civil law tradition, but on cross-examination, the evidence is both the question and the answer combined, and in evaluating a witness's testimony, obviously you want to look at their entire testimony. You look at the documents, and then you're going to look at the other evidence together. Of course, I'm not saying anything that Your Honours don't know, and I apologise for being presumptuous enough to even go into this area, but the Prosecution when you read their brief, it's as if this is a 98 bis proceeding. They ignore everything and then they ask you also ignore the Defence witnesses, ignore them because they're insiders. Well, who else are we going to get? We're trying to figure out how the system worked over there. That's first and foremost. So who am I going to get? Somebody from some other country? Keep in mind, Your Honours, and I can give you the citations, I don't have it right offhand but it's here some place, we'll get to it, throughout the course of this five-year trial we've had Prosecutor after Prosecutor come in and ask, "What's a constituent person? What's a constituent nation?" After five years. Well, if a witness has an answer -- there was one great exchange. The Prosecutor says: "So, there were three groups. Three groups. And you wanted to be constituent nations." And the witness, it was Batinic, by the way, said: "No, we were constituent peoples. We were constituent nations. It's not that we aspired to be, we were." Well, if you don't understand that fundamental principle, then obviously you're going to have some problems. You're going to have some problems that were same way, we submit, that Biden, Vice-President Biden today had, who was a senator back then, and gets elections from Silajdzic in saying: "Well, in Bosnia everybody is Bosnian. Who came up with this idea that there's Serbs and Croats? They're Bosnian Roman Catholic and they're Bosnian Orthodox." And we saw that, and we even see that from other witnesses, and we'll get to that hopefully. Hadzihasanovic said it. And of course if you're not aware that there's a specific characteristic to being a constituent nation in this fragile environment, knowing what is happening around, and knowing the disintegration of Yugoslavia, obviously you're going to have some challenges. The same thing we saw when we came to social ownership. There was one great exchange. I believe it was Ms. West that asked the question, and it was, well, I guess two or three people owned the place. That was her concept of social ownership. And then we see these internationals, which we're going to get to, that come, not a one of them, not one, and I searched, I searched like Diogenes searching for the truth. I searched for one of them to say, "You know what, I read the documents. I read -- I got ahold of the Official Gazettes, I read them, I analysed it, or I had somebody translate them and analyse them to me." Not one single witness of all those internationals that went in theatre, not one of them bothered to look. What happened? They came with their preconceived notion planted in Zagreb, because that was the place where they first arrived to, they got their little orientation, and they were all told, there's Bosnia, there's a map, and there is this place over there, and it's a mini state. It's self-proclaimed. Self-proclaimed. And so that was the beginning. That was how they arrived, with that notion in mind. And we have witnesses and we will get to it who say, well, you know, Dr. Prlic was the president. In my country, or as I understand, a president usually has powers over the minister of defence, the military. So obviously he would have. And by the way, I saw him in a room, and there was the minister of defence. There wasn't a minister. It was a -- the head of the Department of Defence, and there was somebody who was from the Main Staff. So we put two and two together. In my country the president controls the military. He controls the minister. The minister's there. The Main Staff is there. Uh-huh. Go no further. Do no more analysis. With the exception of one, Your Honours; with the exception of one witness, and the witness was BH. With the exception of that witness, every single one said that Dr. Prlic's office was always open. He was always willing to provide information. All they had to do was ask. Now, there was -- there are occasions, and there is one in particular, because I don't want to mislead the Trial Chamber, where Watkins comes in, I believe it was Watkins, who says, "Well, I asked them some information about the exchange of prisoners and some humanitarian aid, and he -- he directed me to other folks, Raguz, and Pusic." Well, those are the subdepartments that deal with those -- those issues. That's why he pushed them. It was also interested -- was also interesting is that -- with Watkins, is that when he comes to meet with Dr. Prlic, he says that Dr. Prlic was just as much interested in finding out what's happening in Central Bosnia, because that's where Watkins was coming from. But my point is this: None of these folks who had access to Dr. Jadranko Prlic every bothered to ask him, "You no what? Tell me how this place works. Tell me about your function, because everybody is a president. Everybody seems to be the head of a department. So how does this work? What is this Presidency? What is a collective body?" I never heard of collective body. I come from a Western country. We have a democratic system, but to assume that just because your system works one way and that everything is going to work the same way in Bosnia-Herzegovina is rather arrogant, and I dare say that we were forced to bring people who would be able to sit down and explain to you how the system functioned. And think about it. We -- we told you that Sarajevo was under siege, that the Central Bank wasn't functioning, that the payment bureau system wasn't functioning. It wasn't functioning because the electrical grid was down, and telecommunications were down, and the entire network was linked. Of course, it would have been nice for the Prosecution to figure that one out on their own before they went ahead and said, "Well, you know, they're trying to Croatise. They're using the Croatian dinar." Well, what was the option? Then we brought in a witness, a gentleman by the name of Primorac. You may recall him. He was almost 7 feet tall. I don't believe Judge Prandler was here at the time. Very tall gentleman, thin. In fact, he was complimented by Mr. Khan here because of his youthful looks. The gentleman was about 70 years old, and Mr. Khan was taken aback when he saw the gentleman's age, birth -- and he was the minister of finance for Bosnia-Herzegovina early on in 1992. Very successful businessman, Ph.D. in economics. And at some point he says, "We had to leave Sarajevo, because you couldn't function there. You couldn't have regular business transactions because of the telecommunications system was down." He talked about the different currencies that were being used; coupons. All right. He's a Croat. Well, you know, he went on. He left and he went to Croatia, and he stayed there. Never got involved in -- in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna or the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. But let's just say for one second that the gentleman provided testimony that was unhelpful or untruthful or that he stretched things a bit, because after all, the Defence may be trying to do that. Did the Prosecution bring in their own expert? Did you ever hear any expert from the Prosecution to rebut the evidence that the Central Bank wasn't functioning? But who else could we bring in? We brought in somebody from Slovenia. Now, he wasn't attacked. At least I wasn't aware that he was lumped in with the other Croats, but he was a Defence witness. But he testified about how the system functioned there. He testified that in their system, the former Yugoslavia, there was this transitional period in how he talked about the collective, and he talked about self-management. It was their way, their system. For better or for worse, it worked for them. And it's -- there is this transition where there's some decentralisation, where power is leaving Belgrade and slowly going to the various republics, and from the republics also there's a great deal of self-management at the municipal level, and they're having to take care of certain functions. And he talked about the funds. He talked about the pension funds, the educational funds, the healthcare fund, and how from the local community taxes would go up and then the funds would be replenished from those taxes. And, of course, his testimony mirrored the testimony that we heard from Tomic. Now, why did it mirror? Because somehow he was connected to the project, to the JCE? No. Because he was from Slovenia, which was part of Yugoslavia, and he grew up and was educated in that system, and he was able to explain exactly how it functioned, and then he was able to have a certain appreciation of the legislation that was coming out of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. He was also able to appreciate the limitations that the folks over there, not just in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna but everywhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Tuzla, Jablanica, else -- the Posavina area. He was able to explain the challenges that they all had because you didn't have the payment bureau functioning, which was a major, major, major institution. It was the bloodline, if you will, for the economy. And so we brought him and we brought in Tomic. Now, of course, Tomic is connected to Prlic because he's part of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. But does that mean that we need to throw out Tomic's testimony completely? He was questioned for days and days on end, and there's one wonderful exchange, I believe we put it into our final brief, where a question was posed by Judge Antonetti, and he tried to explain that part of the purpose was to bring some normality out of this total chaos. The Prosecution would have you believe that everything was being provided for by Sarajevo. Well, was there any evidence to that? Was there any evidence? The only evidence that came out was where we -- we brought in evidence that a bundle of money, new printed money, came out. One-third went to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. It couldn't be used in places like Mostar, because you couldn't use it as hard currency. They shifted over to Central Bosnia, and that's where they were using it. And what am I trying to explain with all of this? What I'm trying to say is before denigrating the -- the Defence witnesses, it might have been good for the Prosecution, first and foremost, to put their case properly before you before making assertion as to Croatisation because of the use of the Croatian dinar. They should have been able to tell you that there was absolutely no need for that, that the Bosnian dinar or Yugoslav dinar or something local was functioning. Did they do that? No. But they had an opportunity afterwards. Nothing prevented them from saying, "You know what, we're going to bring in an expert. We're going is to show the Prlic Defence. We're going to impeach Primorac, who had nothing to -- he wasn't part of this project. We're going to impeach Cvikl, the expert, and we're going to impeach Tomic." Did they bring in on rebuttal? Did they make a submission? No. They had one expert. They never put the expert on. Wonder why. Wonder why. Be circumspect with the Prosecution's evidence as the Prosecution demands, Your Honours, as you be with the Defence evidence. Adopt a zero tolerance for the parsing of words, the creative constrict of theories and conclusion that are based on selective extractions of phrases and text that distort the meaning or deliberately avoid pesky evidence. It seems that the Prosecution has an aversion, has an aversion to evidence that just gets in the way of their theory of the case. I don't mean to make light of it. I mean, this is a very serious occasion, but it just seems to me that as much as they try to portray that there is this huge joint criminal enterprise and that Dr. Prlic is this and Dr. Prlic is that, when you look at their evidence, and I do invite your close scrutiny and attention, we spent the last five weeks, Your Honours, going through their footnotes, and if we are unprepared today, it is because the perfect got in the way of the good. We tried to go through all of the footnotes in order to bring every single -- every single situation where the Prosecution, we believe, stretched the truth a little bit, was trying to be economically frugal with the truth, where they cut a word here, take a phrase there, and try to construct some kind of a narrative. And there's lots of situations, and we're going to go through some of that Your Honours. We won't be able to go through all of them, but we will do that. Now, this is a big case. Mistakes are going to be made. Mistakes are going to be made. They're honest mistakes. They're honourable people on both sides of the aisle, and of course we shouldn't -- no ill-intentions can be drawn from those mistakes, but as Oliver Wendell Holmes Senior, the father of the great jurist -- American jurist Oliver Wendell Holmes Junior, once wrote: Every dog knows the difference between being kicked and stumbled over, and I think that's so. Be mindful. And of course, Mr. Scott was very wise to tell us all, what's sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander, and we're mindful for that. Now, I'm going to begin by going through some of the witnesses in a moment, Your Honours, and I'm not going to spend my time trying to convince you or trying to persuade you, trying to find that you go in my direction. It's a little too late in the game for that. But I am going to try, hopefully, to get the members of the Trial Chamber to have an abiding appreciation of the record and to simply raise the consciousness of skepticism, so that after you hear all of the closing arguments and after you've read all the final briefs, and you begin the hard task of going through the record, that you do so with this current of skepticism permeating throughout your consciousness. That's the best, I think, I can achieve at this point, nothing more. And as I said, what I have said is not evidence, although I am trying very hard to demonstrate that there's more than a well-crafted brief. There's more than a nice speech. You have to look at the evidence. Now, all of these internationals, and I'm going to begin with them, as I said, had one thing in common. They virtually all came totally uninformed. They virtually all came and found Dr. Prlic's office open and ready to provide them with information. When they came to testify, virtually all of them -- not all of them. Most of them, I should say, had these narratives that had been prepared. And the one that I want to focus on most to start with, although the witness is by no means the exception, is Witness BA, Witness BA. Over a period of four days, the Prosecution sits with the witness, provides the witness documents, provides the witness documents the witness has never seen, and then over a period of four days a narrative with titles, subtitles, sub-subtitles, is prepared. There is a draft, there is another draft, until we just get it right. Now, we then present that statement here, and we move it into evidence because we're going to save some time. Major witness; save some time. Four days getting that statement just right. Comma in the right place, right adjective. Here's a document, and if you haven't seen it, who knows, it might help you, just might help you refresh your memory. And I submit that if this were to occur in any of our jurisdictions, that statement would be thrown out of court. That would not be acceptable as a statement, even if the witness were to come in and say, "I adopt that statement." Why? Because is it really the witness's statement? Now, imagine if we were in a country where you have an investigative judge, and the investigative judge during the investigation comes up with a witness, and rather than ask the question, get the answer, question, answer, question, answer, write it down or tape record it, I mean imagine all the millions of dollars we're spending, we don't even get a tape recording, okay, never mind a video, that's asking for a bit too much, but we could tape record at least. So imagine now you had this investigative judge, and he spent four days showing some documents to the witness, letting information creep into the memory of the witness, drafting the statement of the witness, and then saying to the witness, "Here, could you take a look at it and see if you need to edit it a little bit?" And even in those instances, the witness would come and then have to re-edit again, but imagine if that were to happen again. How much value would that statement have? Zero. What's the purpose of showing a witness documents that the witness has never seen when you're there to extract information? Who? What? Where? Why? How? Explain. Describe. Those are the magic questions that any good investigator needs to act. Not "Here are some documents. I know you haven't seen them. I know you haven't seen them, but hey, maybe that will jiggle your memory. Maybe you'll come up with something." And then there's Witness BB, for instance. There's one -- one exchange where Witness BB is commenting on a document that wasn't produced by BB. It was produced by somebody else, and it's unclear whether that somebody else was actually at the meeting describing the events of the meeting, and if it weren't for some questioning from the Bench, one would never know that. It comes out from the Bench there's a question because sometimes, despite all our complaints, and I must say I've been humbled having read the record. Sometimes you think you're hearing things, but when you see them on paper it's a little bit different, because maybe the heat of the moment all these other distractions are going on. Some of the Judges' questions are right on point. They come out and they say, "Wait a second. There's something doesn't quite look right," and then the witness says, "Well, I wasn't at the meeting." Yet the witness now has testified about the meeting. Or, for instance, where you have another witness, and this would be BH, who puts quotation marks, and when pressed, "Was that a quote?" "Well, it was the essence of what was said." "Well, how do we know whether it was actually said?" "Well, it's close enough." "Did you put the quotations marks there?" "No." "Who did?" "Well, the person who was taking the statement." Well, how do we know when it's a quote and when it's not a quote? And of course, it may sound like an old Defence trick, which it's not, when asked, "Well, can you produce some notes? Did you have any notes?" Yes, the witness had notes. "Can you produce them? Can you produce those notes so we can see what's in your statement that you drafted over a period of days with the ICTY investigator and the documents, documents again that you're seeing that you'd never seen before, it might help you with your narrative, can we see the notes?" And the answer is, "No." All right. Some never had notes. Some have come in and said, "You know what? I just can't remember. It's been 15 years." Well, I can understand that. I think we all can understand that. Some of us can't remember what happened two days ago. But then on a critical point, "Ah, that will never leave my mind. This is exactly what was said." Okay. Fair enough. It's one of those things, you know, like me being able to recall certain events in the courtroom. All right. Well, can we see a report, something? Do we have notes? No notes. Okay. Fine. How about a report? How about let's do a little -- do a little foundation. "Were you required to provide information up the chain," you know, "on important meetings?" "Yes." "And when something significant was heard, were you required to put that into your report?" "Yes." "And would you have done that?" "Well, most likely." "Okay. Most likely, I'll take that. All right." Now, and here's the million dollar question: "Can you please help me out here. Not that I doubt you, but show me a document. Show me some place because, you know what, with some of these institutions, the Defence does not have access to their files." They don't have access to their archives, and Your Honours know that very well. So if you're going to say something, back it up. "Well, I might have written or I must have written." "Okay. Well, you gave a statement to the Prosecution." You would think that the Prosecutor or the investigator, actually, because they're not there or maybe they might have been there, would have asked a logical question, "Well, do you have -- where's the report?" Because this would be the smoking gun. We've got Dr. Prlic using the "ethnic cleansing" words. So where's the document? Well, there is no document. I can't remember what was said. I can't even remember if I wrote a report, but I remember those words. Those are the examples of the internationals, and there are more, and more will come. We seem to place a lot of currency on somebody being an international, when, in fact, they're no better or no different from anyone else. You have BF, for instance. BF comes and says, "Well, we couldn't open up an office in Mostar, we, the organisation." I'm not mentioning organisations. I'm told that as long as I don't mention organisations and the gender, I'm more or less safe, and if I'm not safe, somebody let me know. "We weren't allowed to open up." Well, okay. That's in direct examination. Then we pressed the witness. "Show me concretely. Show me concretely where you wrote a report, where you made a request, and you made a request to Dr. Prlic and he said no." "Well, it wasn't like that." "Well, how was it?" "Well, it was a feeling that I got. It was an impression." "Well, did you ever ask?" "Well, it was unsafe." "Well, okay, it was unsafe. You were told it was unsafe?" "Yes, but you didn't need to be told because you could see it all around you." And then we find out after cross-examination, full circle, that effectively the question was never popped. In other words, may we open an office? But instead through innuendo the witness wanted you to believe that Dr. Prlic was not providing them access to have an office in Mostar. Now, where I come from, a half -- half a truth is a half a lie, and half a lie is a lie. Now, I'm not suggesting that the gentleman was lying, but I am suggesting that he was not being totally candid, because he was leaving the impression with the Trial Chamber, because -- the witness was leaving an impression with the Trial Chamber that the organisation could not open an office. There's another -- another witness. Another international comes in, and let me get away from these initials because despite all my efforts I'm bound to slip up, let's talk about Ray Lane. Wonderful gentleman, great sense of humour, you might recall. Fellow from Ireland. He came and he testified. And he arrived in situ in around December 1992. That's when he first arrives in Mostar. So he, like everyone else from his organisation - and he testified in public - he shows up. He's with ECMM. And he shows up. He's had two days or so of some sort of an orientation in Zagreb, which he says it was not really much of an orientation. And, in fact, on cross-examination it was, like, "Well, here's a map. You go down that road, you're bound to run into Mostar, or at least Bosnia. You go -- you just head -- just head in that direction. Can't miss it." And when he arrives there, it takes him about two weeks, according to his testimony, to find out that the Muslims are on the east side. And it took him two weeks -- or ten days to two weeks to walk across the bridge. All right. He's questioned, because he had some pretty harsh characterisations of Dr. Prlic. In his statement, it was a two-day statement that he gave. They went to Ireland, spent two days. Then he had -- it was over a weekend, and then he spent some time. They gave him the draft, and then they said, "Look it over and correct it. Take your time. Be thorough." And you might find -- when I was cross-examining him, because of the type of work that he does in the military, I suggested that he was meticulous, and there was some bantering about that. In any event, he gives the statement, and in the statement, of course when he comes, he has to correct it because even his own rank was wrong in the statement itself, among other things, but one of the things that he said was that Dr. Prlic would dine at his private restaurant. Now, when you read the statement, it's pretty graphic, graphic in the sense that you read it and you know that whoever wrote it, wrote it with purpose in mind, so that the reader would have just the right emotion, the right feeling about. So there he is, Dr. Prlic's private restaurant, and here comes the private waiter in a tuxedo and delivers the food. And there we are. It's in Mostar, and it's up on this building that's overlooking the city or parts of the city. Turns out on cross-examination that he's at Hotel Ero. Hotel Ero is where Dr. Prlic had his office. And in the hotel, like most hotels, there's a restaurant. And like most hotels with a restaurant, there's room service. So you have the -- you call down to the restaurant and you order up a meal. They put it on a tray, come up the elevator. Normally in that part of the world waiters wear a little black suit and the bow tie. He shows up. Uh-huh. I'm having a private dinner in a private restaurant of the president, and now it's in the statement. Now, if the ICTY investigator had any moxie, had any understanding of his craft, he would have said, hey, wait a second. Where is that restaurant? And by the time they got to this gentleman with all the information they had, and -- but keep in mind that this case has been an ongoing saga for this Tribunal because there are other cases behind it for many, many, many years, and Mostar is not that far away, and they paid a lot of visits down there, so you would think that the investigator would know right off the bat that that's not quite accurate or would press him. "Where is it? Show me. Describe to me the location about this private restaurant." And you would think that an investigator would also -- who is investigating the case would ask around and they would find out very quickly that Dr. Prlic never owned a restaurant in Mostar, but this is in -- this is now into their -- into the statement. Then the gentleman says that, "I'm talking to Dr. Prlic. I'm having a conversation, one of these discussions, and he pulls out a map," and there's this wonderful exchange, because later on he says, "Well, I'm jogging on the beach of Scheveningen, and lo and behold it's not a map. It's a drawing. It's not a map, a drawing." Now, some of us may be able to make that kind of mistake, but a military guy, an officer? I put that question to him, and he kind of joked by saying that the most dangerous thing that you can see an officer do is have a map in his hands. All right. Let's forgive him for that. And he says that Dr. Prlic drafts -- makes a circle, draws a line through the circle, and says, "This is how we're going to carve up Bosnia-Herzegovina. One side for the Serbs, one side for the Croats." All right. Now, he's a military guy. He's there to observe. He's there to collect information. Dr. Prlic is -- is forthright, and you would think -- you would think that the gentleman would say, "Okay. Can I have that drawing?" We don't have the drawing. He remembers it. And then we see this drawing again come up, and we see it in the Prosecution's brief, in a footnote. I believe it's in a footnote, or it might even be in a text, where the Prosecution says it looked remarkably similar, remarkably similar to the one that Paddy Ashdown drew when he was meeting with Tudjman. I believe it was 1995. I think it was in -- I can't remember exactly where the event -- where -- it was in London. Thank you. And according to Paddy Ashdown, copious wine was being poured, and there they were having this discussion, and that's when -- and he pops the question to Tudjman where does he see Bosnia-Herzegovina ten years from now, and then supposedly on a napkin there is this drawing. Well, guess what, Your Honours? We don't have that. We don't have the drawing. We don't have the napkin. We haven't seen it. But it's remarkably similar. This is what the Prosecution wants you to believe. And regarding that particular piece of evidence, and you may wish to look into it, I don't know whether it was an oversight, I don't know whether there's some contradiction, the Prosecution moved to have the Trial Chamber accept as part of the -- as a -- to judiciously notice -- adjudicated fact, thank you, something that came in from a previous case regarding the Paddy Ashdown napkin incident, you know. So from a judgement, this is an adjudicated fact. Well, the Prosecution had moved for the testimony or the statement from the gentleman, from Paddy Ashdown, and the Trial Chamber, in fact, made a decision on that. It was on a 92 bis decision. I must be driving Ms. Tomanovic nuts because I'm going all over the script now. Anyway, it was 19 October 2006 where the Chamber found, and this is what I'm a little bit confused about, but I'm sure Your Honours will be able to get through it, on page 3 it says: "Considering that the testimony refers to a single conversation that Mr. Ashdown had with Franjo Tudjman and then president of the Republic of Croatia, the then president on 6 May 1995, considering that during the conversation Franjo Tudjman expressed his views of how Bosnia would look ten years later, that is, in 2005, considering that he also made remarks about Mr. Izetbegovic, the then president of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Bosnian Muslims, considering, however, that the testimony provides information only about Franjo Tudjman's frame of mind in 1995 and not about the period covered in the indictment, considering consequently that the testimony is irrelevant, irrelevant, for this case," and it dismisses the motion. And -- now, this was -- Your Honours, this was of 19 October 2006, and the adjudicated fact came in -- and if I may be of some assistance to the Trial Chamber, although you're probably on top of everything, I believe that would be 7 September 2006 where, I believe, the Trial Chamber accepted as adjudicated fact, and there is a little table to it, it's 42, where it says: "Having sketched on the back of a menu a rough map of the former Yugoslavia showing the situation in ten years, Franjo Tudjman explained to Mr. Ashdown that one part of Bosnia would belong to Croatia and the other part to Serbia." Blaskic trial judgement, para 106. Anyway, I leave that for you to consider, and, Your Honours, I believe we might be coming up to the break. If not I'll continue, but for me to it would be a good time at this point, but I can continue. I'm in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's almost time for the break, so we will have our traditional 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Now, I want to turn my attention -- turn our attention to -- to Witness BA in -- a little more in depth. The witness testified based on the witness's observations that Mr. Prlic, for instance, was fluent in English, yet we saw last week a video by Ms. Giles, that was a 40-minute video-tape that was shown, and then when she was cross-examined, she admitted that his English was not the best and there was a problem with communication. Also, you have a tape that was transcribed. A witness came in and testified. We will be getting to her in a -- perhaps later in the afternoon, and from there you could also see that Dr. Prlic had problems with his English. It's hardly fluent, as Witness BA said. Now, juxtapose that with witness, for instance -- I believe it was BF. Witness BF testified, and though Witness BF was fluent in English, insisted on testifying in his own language, and the reason that he gave was because of the nuances of the -- of the language and wanted to make sure that what was being said was being accurately transcribed, that the witness was not being misinterpreted. I mention that just as a little vignette. Witnesses that come here, we afford them the best translation services, and even when they are fluent in English, the witnesses are entitled to speak in their own language, as they should, because the witnesses understand the need for precision. And then you have reports -- or you have testimony from witnesses, and then they affix meanings, impressions, conclusions, sometimes they even put quotes. When dealing with individuals such as Dr. Prlic, who is hardly fluent in English, and this, by the way -- you would find this on transcript page 7334 regarding the witness's impression that Dr. Prlic was fluent. Now, the witness also was questioned about the situation in Zenica and in Central Bosnia, and one of the themes that was running through the Prosecution witnesses, particularly BA, BB, BC, you name it, you know, BD, BF, one of the things was everything was safe and sound for the Croats in Zenica, yet none of them were there. None of them went over there to take a look and see what's happening. And when reports were being made to them about the situation, those reports were merely being dismissed as ploys for reverse ethnic cleansing. Some were pressed about the Mujahedin. Some were aware; some were not aware. But we submit you have to take that into consideration, especially when they're pressed on cross-examination, and they're being asked whether they actually went there, whether they knew what was happening to the Croats. Their answer always was, "Well, as far as we knew, as far as what we were told by our headquarters in Zenica, everything was fine." And of course, if there's reverse ethnic cleansing happening from Central Bosnia, and Zenica is supposed to be the place that's supposed to be covering this area, and the Prosecution is trying to convince you that the Croats -- or that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was involved in reverse ethnic cleansing, one would think that you would go to the source. The source is Zenica. The source is not Mostar to have somebody look at some documents who wasn't in situ, who didn't prepare the documents, to come in and say all was fine with the Croats in Zenica. And Witness BA was also questioned about a particular piece of legislation that had come out on the use of abandoned property, and this was the beginning of sort of a repeated mantra by all the Prosecution witnesses, all the international witnesses who were there. None of them actually read, actually read, and analysed the legislation. None of them actually went to see what was happening elsewhere. And in this particular instance, the legislation I'm talking about, and I'm going to speak more about it, hopefully, with BB, but one of the documents is P01894, but you may recall there was a great deal of testimony back that we had in 2006 about a particular piece of legislation coming out -- this decision coming out of Mostar, where supposedly based on this decision, approximately 10.000 Muslim refugees were denied access to humanitarian aid. And this is what that decision was all about. And the purpose was to drive these refugees outside of Mostar. And of course when you look at the decision and you look at the testimony that was taken, and in particular with this -- with this witness we're talking about pages 7430 onwards, all the way to -- to -- I think it's, I believe, 7436, what is noted is that first of all, the decision did not discriminate. Mostar also had Croat refugees. When pressed, the witness did not know how many Croat refugees were in Mostar, yet the conclusion that was jumped on was that this was an exquisite opportunity to get rid of -- of the -- of the Muslim refugees, and of course, somehow it's been tied into the events of May 9, 1993. On page 7353, the witness says that -- the witness was unaware of how many refugees went to Croatia; on 7351, how many Croat refugees were -- versus Muslim refugees were in that vicinity. And the witness was highly educated. And if I'm permitted to at least state the education, had gone to law school. The same thing with BB. They had both gone to law school. And what's important about this is here we're talking about a piece of legislation, you know, as crude as it may be, and the question turns on interpretation. Well, first of all, you'd think that you'd want to get ahold of it and analyse it like a lawyer. There was some sort of an exchange. There was an objection to the fact that the individual hadn't practiced law. Well, so what? Hopefully law school turns out people that know how to read the law. That's the whole purpose. But where did the interpretation came from? It came if Merhamet, a NGO organisation, not in the business of law, where supposedly there was -- based on their interpretation, there was going to be massive discrimination. And then, of course, there's an exchange of letters by somebody very high up and Mate Boban, where Mate Boban is explaining exactly the purpose behind this piece of legislation. And in particular, based on this legislation, you see that persons of the age of 17 to 60, and women, I believe, up to 55, are excluded. Why? Well, there was a war, and you had the All People's Defence, and everybody was mobilised, and that was universal, and everybody was aware of it. And at the beginning, as described in Mate Boban's letter in response, that this is exactly what they were told: Exclude these people. And incidentally, everywhere, all over Bosnia-Herzegovina, the same thing is happening. And it's not a tu quoque argument, because we're suggesting that based on the then existing system in the former Yugoslavia and in Bosnia, you had this All People's Defence. You had the JNA or the military forces, and then you had your Territorial Defence. Everybody had either work obligation or had to -- had to serve in some capacity. There was a state of war, and as a result, folks, men in particular, aged 17 or 18 to 60, had to serve in one capacity or another. And you will see later on that when there's a load of refugees -- a load of displaced persons, I should say, because we've been losing that term rather loosely in this courtroom, but we're talking about in a sense the refugees being displaced from their own locations. When you have a load of them coming, and these are Croats, and they're heading towards Croatia because Herzegovina, in particular the area of -- of Mostar and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, is saturated, it can no longer absorb any more, and so Croats are going to Croatia as they had been going all along, the men, the military-aged men are taken and separated, because they have to do their duty. And I believe we also saw some testimony and some documents where even the -- the Bosnian -- the BiH I should say, embassy, in Zagreb was urging that the men of military age, the Muslim men of military age, be forced to return to Bosnia in order to take up the cause. And incidentally, the letter I was referring to by Mr. Boban is 1D01188. Now, as far as when it comes to -- when it comes to the issue of this reverse ethnic cleansing, we do invite the Trial Chamber to also consider documents 1D00936 and 1D00937. And because of the time, I don't have -- time does not allow me to spend much time with these documents, but if we just look at one -- at 1D00936. I don't know if we have it on the e-court, if it's available. You'll see on the second page and onwards a list -- a list, and you see the numbers, and you see the locations, and then you can draw your own conclusions, Your Honour. Don't accept what Karnavas says. Don't accept what the Prosecution say. Look at the documents. Look at the record. And then when we look at 1D00937, on the second page, at paragraph 8 it says: "Now more than a thousand Croats have left Konjic. There will be a real danger that in a next step the Muslim are going to expel the about 500 Croats still living in Jablanica as received from the reports and from our own former activities, Jablanica becomes more and more isolated." This is not about fixing blame as to who's responsible for what. The bottom line is that you have all these refugees coming, all these people being displaced, leaving out of fear, leaving because they're isolated, leaving because they've heard about the Mujahedin, leaving because they are in these enclaves, and yet the recurring theme of the Prosecution is they're all being forced to leave. And then when you ask someone like BA or BB or BC, "Okay. You go there? Did you see how the situation was?" All of them say, "No." Concerning BA, I also want to touch a little bit on transit centres, and that would be in Prosecution's brief 454 and 455. And again I must apologise for rushing through this, but time does not permit me to dilly-dally on anything in particular, but we would suggest and we would submit that if you look at, for instance, footnote -- footnote 1052 of the Prosecution's brief, and then you compared that with paragraph 51 of P09712, which is the report -- or the statement by and with BA, and the investigators, you will see that it's a virtual lifting. Oh, there's a little change of a word here or there, but it's a virtual lifting. And the same happens on footnote 1054, and you compared the text, for instance, in paragraph 453. It's -- it's amazing. And I raise this because as I indicated earlier, when drafting the report, when drafting the statement, it would appear, Your Honours, it would appear that the drafter of the statement had the final brief in mind. We submit that you should look at the final brief that was submitted by the Prlic Defence, paragraph 193 to 222. We also suggest that you look at, for instance, among other documents, P03394, and on this document, if I could just spend a moment or two. We see that this is a document generated on 12 July 1993, and if we go to page 3 on this document -- it's not paginated, Your Honours, but it's on page 3. Towards the bottom of the middle of the page and downwards we see the following text: "Having set up an analysis department at the end of March, we were able to complete the data on expelled refugees and displaced persons, and we now have reports from 5 May 1993, 23 June, and 8 July 1993. In the first period (5 May 1993), both Muslim and Croats became expelled persons because of Serbian aggression, and since June there has been a significant increase in the number of expelled Croats because of the Muslim offensive in Central Bosnia and north-eastern Herzegovina. "Thus the numbers of expelled Croats residing in HZ-HB has increased by 50.000 (i.e., 100 per cent) and now totals -- and now totals 110.061. It is unlikely that new expelled persons will be arriving in this area. Also note that there are around 120.000 Croats who had been expelled from Bosanska Posavina, and who have been housed outside HZ-HB, which brings the total number of Croats who have been driven out, expelled, or displaced from BiH to around 270.000 or 35 per cent, according to the 1991 census." And this was document P03394. I also invite the Trial Chamber to look at 1D00929, P03796, and see also P03990, page 9, para 37. And if I may get that for a second, then maybe I can read it, read part of it. And all I'm trying to demonstrate, Your Honours, is that there's -- there are two sides to the story. Unfortunately, the internationals are only coming here and telling one side, or at least some of them. And for whatever reason, it would appear that, for instance, to borrow a phrase from the Prosecution or their expert, command climate. If they arrive in Zagreb or they arrive wherever the focal point is, before coming into country and into location, they're being told that this is a self-proclaimed entity that is committing ethnic cleansing, that is cleansing itself -- if that's how you start, that's your orientation, that's your grounding before you get there, and then if you're not clever or not energetic or just simply overwhelmed with the situation and don't take the one or two steps further into the situation to look around and observe and ask questions, then perhaps everything that you're going to report may be off-skewed, a little bit off the mark. And then when considering, and we have testimony, Your Honours, that all these internationals are bunking around together, they're sharing offices, they're passing information and they're passing it as if they're the originator of the information when, in fact, it's the same source. We saw that. And I'm not saying it's happening all the time, but if you have five sources saying the same thing but it's one source, actually, it's easy to then jump to the conclusion that, "Well, see? You know, there's verification. There's validation." And so we're urging the Trial Chamber to be very, very cautious. Look at all the documents, don't be dismissive the way the Prosecution suggests you should be. Instead, they're interested in to jumping into conclusions and making reports, and then those reports are moved up the ladder, and now you have this belief that somehow this is how the system worked. We see president, and you'll see this -- there's a wonderful exchange with -- with -- actually with BF, who indicates that, well, BF's understanding is that the president has capacity over the military and that's the end of the story. Now, let's move on to BD. BD is the witness that claimed that Dr. Jadranko Prlic provided the -- the pass. BD was questioned and cross-examined extensively. In one of the reports you might remember BD describes a certain event as the successful Muslim offensive. I believe that was the term that was used. BD claimed that her -- the organisation that BD worked for, and BD in particular, was prevented from setting up an office in Mostar. And then when questioned extensively, it turns out that BD complained that she was never given assistance to find and locate a place to rent. That's a far cry from being prohibited from opening up an office. BD also explained that she had a -- BD had a wonderful explanation on direct knowledge. Direct knowledge is when, for instance, you speak to somebody who purportedly has direct knowledge and that person tells you. So from direct to direct. Usually that's called hearsay, and the problem with hearsay is, well, sometimes it's good, and sometimes it's bad. Now, this is -- I make light of it a little bit, but it's almost sad, sad that you write reports based on what you're being told, but you take it on and you write it as if you've observed it, and you say, "I had direct knowledge of these events." Well, how is it? "Well, I spoke to somebody who had direct knowledge." Well, how do you know that person had direct knowledge? The only way that you would know is, A, you have some independent indicia; or B, you saw the person getting -- absorbing the direct knowledge. The same witness, and we're talking about in the transcript 20808 to 20810. The -- this witness was questioned about the situation in Central Bosnia, because again the witness, under the impression that there's reverse ethnic cleansing, and of course BD never visited Central Bosnia, Vares, Busovaca, Vitez, Gornji Vakuf, Kakanj, never went there. But BD was located and her work space was with another organisation, and they shared information, and that comes across in the cross-examination. She testified 4 July -- 3 July, 4 July we see the testimony. I suggest there's -- there's a wonderful exchange when -- when I asked BD if this witness had met Mate Boban, because, of course, she -- the witness is claiming to -- to know the levers of power, and there's a wonderful exchange where the witness says, "Thanks God, no." I suggest -- I submit, Your Honours, that it would be -- it would be a good opportunity for the Trial Chamber to wind back and look at that particular video and look at the expression on the witness's face, and that -- that expression says it all. The same witness talked about the water situation and talked about an exchange that Dr. Prlic had concerning the water situation, because the myth was, and I say "myth," the myth was that one of the reasons there was no water on the east side was because the Croats on the west side had done everything possible to prevent water from going there. And -- and, of course, it turns out that this witness, BD, was utterly ignorant, utterly uninformed of anything that had to do with water. And documents were presented to the witness, and you will see this on pages 20897 to 20901 where we showed 1D01566, 1D01567, 1D01568. And then, of course, there is -- there's an interesting -- there is an interesting passage in the transcript, and that is on, I believe, on page 2000 -- 20000 and -- one second, Your Honours. It's 20909 and it goes on to 20910, and it more or less sums up what I've been trying to say here today in part, and that is that the internationals are coming. They're coming uninformed. They don't know the situation. They're not bothering to -- to find out the facts, yet they all come, and they all have one thing on their mind, an opinion, and they start with that opinion that they received from somebody else, and that's the end of the search that they do, and from there they go on. Now, this witness also talked about the milk convoys, and it's in paragraphs 493 and 498 of the Prosecution's brief. And what I -- what I suggest, Your Honours, because I'm running out of time, of course, that first you look at the Makarska Agreement, which is rather clear. That's P10264. Look at Simunovic's testimony as well -- I'm sorry. Look at P03346. Look at 1D02070, because this was advertised. Also look at from Witness DZ, the documents that were shown, P03420, P03428. DZ's testimony of 24 January 2008, 26736 to 26741. Also look at P03539, 1D01870. And with this particular witness, that is BD, also look at P03420, P03428, 1D01336, P03453. Time doesn't permit me to go into all of this, Your Honours, but one of the issues concerning the milk convoys, if I can just sort of state our position, which we believe is supported by the evidence, and testimony was heard, and you have the documents before you, and you have to look at more than one witness for this, we heard last week from the Prosecution that humanitarian aid wasn't going forward because there was this constant blocking or constant -- agreements were signed and then the Croats would attack. The Makarska Agreement was a fairly big deal. You had Granic who was the minister of foreign affairs come down, and he took part in that. And no sooner than the agreement was signed, then you have an offensive by the ABiH which effectively blocked the passage of the convoys. And of course there was reporting, there was sort of mixed reporting, it's rather clear who initiated the attack, and we submit that the evidence is rather overwhelming that it was the Muslim forces that initiated the attack, but this is an exquisite example. You can't have -- you can't have it both ways. You can't say, "Well, the humanitarian convoys are not coming in, the HVO is to blame," when, in fact, you initiate -- you initiate an attack that obviously is going to cause a response, and then say, "See, there goes the HVO, there goes the HZ-HB, there go the Croats again. They're trying to starve the Muslims in Mostar on the east side." It's these sorts of games. And when you look at BD's testimony, Your Honours, and I submit, I truly submit, and I saw this with all due humility, and I'm cautious to -- I'm cautious to -- to say this, but over the past five years we see a lot of legal officers who have -- and it's no great secret that they've summarised testimony as the case is going along. The problem with summarising the testimony is it takes a long time to understand these -- these facts. It takes a long time to understand this story, and it may be that during the course of the next six or eight months or a year, or however long it takes you, that I strongly urge the Trial Chamber to go over the entire testimony again. It's tedious, sometimes boring, but it's essential. We've had to do this in the last few months. But going back to the milk convoy, the attack blocked the road towards Croatia. That was my point that I was trying to make, and because they blocked --
